text: The Stolen Rooster

As you leave, a villager runs after you accusing one of your soldiers of stealing a rooster. A few squawks silence the culprit's attempt to deny the crime. Honor requires you to uphold the laws of the land, but your soldiers expect a generous {RANK} to value those who shed blood for {PRONOUN} over those who do not.
Return the rooster and have the thief whipped.
Tell the villager that the rooster is just part of the debt owed to their protectors.
Throw the villager some {COIN} in compensation.
No Welcome for the Afflicted

As you prepare to leave, a delegation of townsfolk approaches you. A band of the sick has camped before the walls and begs passers-by for alms. The townsfolk fear the sickness will spread and, at any rate, say the beggars are frightening away customers.
Tell the townsfolk that their compassion is being tested before {GODS}, and that they should treat the sick with kindness.
Give the sick some {COIN} and food on the condition that they seek a more welcoming town elsewhere.
Drive the sick away, telling them they must have wronged the world grievously to be so afflicted.
Do not get involved.
No Place for the Sick

As you make ready to leave, a delegation of townsfolk comes to you. A pack of the sick has camped before the walls, begging for scraps. The townsfolk fear the sickness will spread and say the beggars are scaring off trade.
Order the townsfolk to leave the sick in peace and treat them with kindness.
Give the sick some {COIN} and food on the condition that they find a more welcoming town elsewhere.
Drive the sick away, telling them only the weak fall to such afflictions.
Do not get involved.
Arrow-Proofing
As you leave the village, one of your soldiers proudly shows you a charmed oil bought from a peddler, who swore that anyone who anoints themselves with it will not be wounded in battle.
Congratulate the soldier on the wise purchase, and say you expect to see them in the thick of the fray in the next battle.
Tell your soldiers they should rely on their own strength instead of charms.
Chastise the soldier for being so gullible.
Glanders Outbreak

As you leave the village, you notice one of your horses has a swollen head and a bloody nose. You know this disease. It can spread to your soldiers, and not only this animal is at risk but every other animal that drank from the same trough.
Kill the horse and the two other horses that shared its stable.
Kill the horse alone, hoping for the best.
Allow the rider to care for the animal, even though it puts them and others at risk.
Lice and Fleas

Lice are part of military life, but several of your soldiers are crawling with the vermin. Perhaps they are especially fierce in these parts, or perhaps they thrive in this weather. You fear they will spread camp fever or worse.
Force the afflicted to shave every strand of their hair and beard.
Make your soldiers go through the laborious work of picking their bodies and clothes clean.
Tell your soldiers to give themselves a good scratch and keep marching.
Donative Demand

It has not escaped your soldiers' notice that you have gathered a fair sum in your treasury. A delegation approaches you and suggests this would be a good time for the traditional donative, as warlords of old were known to give their companies.
Convince your soldiers that the {COIN} would be better spent on supplies and recruits to ensure their survival.
Tell your soldiers they can do as they wish with their wages, but you are not in the habit of subsidizing wine sellers, dubious company and gambling sharks more than necessary.
I am a river of wealth unto you, my brave warriors!
Erupt in a towering rage, so they will think twice about bothering you again.
Buried Splendors

One of your soldiers comes to you excitedly. A peddler in the marketplace sold them a map to a treasure buried by a long-dead sorcerer in a dry gully near here. They want a little time to check it out and promise you a fifth share of anything they find. You have heard tales of gold in ancient tombs hereabouts, but you would give a hundred to one odds that this leads to a grave pillaged centuries ago or someone's underground cistern, and the locals will not welcome a soldier smashing things up with pick and shovel.
Tell them that no one sells maps to treasure they could just as easily dig up themselves.
Indulge your soldier, and wait for the errand to be done.
Tell them the old sorcerers sealed wights into their treasure chambers with the power to turn a soul's skin inside out, and you cannot possibly let them go.
Tempting Berries
Your company stumbles upon bushes of ripe berries near a village, a welcome break on the journey. You have not seen berries quite like these before, but they do look tasty.
Let your soldiers pick some berries from the bushes.
The bushes may belong to someone. Leave them to the local farmers.
If they are ripe, why have animals or villagers not already taken them? They might be poisonous. Avoid them.
Honor the Slain Foe
Your {CULTURE_NAME} troops ask to take charge of the {CULTURE_BURIAL_STYLE} of the {CULTURE_NAME} in the enemy's ranks, saying they owe a duty to their kin even if those kin fought in a bad cause.
Refuse, knowing that separate rites will breed suspicion among the different peoples in your ranks.
Grant their request, as there is no shame in honoring a valiant foe.
Respect for the Fallen
Your {CULTURE_NAME} warriors ask to see to the {CULTURE_BURIAL_STYLE} of the {CULTURE_NAME} in the enemy's ranks, saying they owe their kin that much even if those kin fought for the wrong side.
Refuse; separate rites would breed suspicion among the different tribes in your ranks.
Grant their request; a valiant foe has earned it.
Ice March

Now that the fighting has ended, you notice the weather has turned bitterly cold and a wind is rising. Soon after you return to the march, several of your soldiers have fallen behind. The rest are shivering in the wind and in no mood to wait. You can march on and hope the stragglers catch up, or set a slower pace.
Continue at a normal marching pace.
Slow down until the stragglers can catch up.
No Mood for Mercy

It was a hard-fought battle, and among your fallen is a young, good-natured {TROOP_TYPE} who kept the spirits of their comrades up in hard times. Your soldiers' faces are grim as they go out to collect the wounded of both sides. You can tell that, if they have their way, few wounded enemies will be brought back to camp alive as prisoners.
Demand that your soldiers respect the customs of war and tend to those who gave quarter.
Remind your soldiers that war is war, the {TROOP_TYPE} knew the risks, and prisoners bring ransoms.
Tell your soldiers they may avenge their comrade as they see fit.
No Mood for Mercy

It was a hard-fought battle, and among your fallen is a young, cheerful {TROOP_TYPE} who kept the spirits of their comrades up in hard times. Your warriors' faces are grim as they go out to collect the wounded of both sides. You can tell that, if they have their way, few wounded enemies will be dragged back to camp alive as captives.
Order your warriors to spare those who yielded and tend to them.
Remind your warriors that war is war, the {TROOP_TYPE} knew the risks, and captives bring a price.
Tell your warriors they can settle the score for their fallen comrade as they like.
Singing for Supper

A wandering bard offers to compose an epic ballad about your heroic deeds, which could raise your renown for a little coin. Do you accept the offer, and if so, do you give any guidance on what to sing?
Let the bard do it and reward them generously, but tell them to describe your losses and faults as well.
You do not need a bard to recount your heroic deeds.
Shower the bard with {COIN} and tell them to feel free to embellish your story as they see fit.

Tragic tales are always the most popular. Make sure the bard leaves out neither the doom that sits on your shoulder, nor your bouts of madness, nor {HOLY_PERSON} who foretold your terrible but heroic death.
Intriguing Rumors

A stranger dressed as a servant of a noble house approaches you. "I hear that you and {RIVALLORD.NAME} are not on the best of terms. Well, what can you expect from someone who cannot keep their own household in order? I was recently employed there, and I know the spouse was unusually close to a stable hand... I can spread the word, if you make it worth my while."
You will not sully anyone's good name with an obviously false rumor.
People will believe the former servant of a noble house. The stranger's favor is worth a purse of {COIN} to you.
Crack a few jokes to your soldiers at {RIVALLORD.NAME}'s expense, but otherwise do nothing.
Ennoble a Fighter

After the battle, one of your {TROOPS} approaches you, dreaming of riding with your cavalry as a {NOBLE_TIER}. They have the money to buy a horse, and they certainly distinguished themselves in the fight. You know however that this will go down badly with the high-born riders, who prefer to mingle with their own class, and probably even more so with their comrades, who will think they scorn them.
Courage and skill deserve a reward, even if the result is not what you hoped.
Explain your reservations, even though you can tell they will not like to hear them, and let them make up their own mind.
Commend them, but tell them to stick with their comrades.
Fertility Festival

The village has seen an unexpected rise in births. Some of your villagers ask your permission to hold a festival in honor of the old harvest mother, keeper of cradle and field. The wise never blessed her rites, and many call her worship a rustic holdover. Her festivals tend to be raucous, as befits fertility, and rather expensive. It would certainly set tongues wagging in the district. Do you grant permission?
A vat of wine to dance in, in honor of the harvest mother!
Give the villagers a stern lecture on the importance of sound custom and lawful worship.
Tell the villagers to keep things discreet.
Educational Advancements

Villagers say that a wanderer has recently arrived and offered to teach their children to read. The stranger is well-educated and has a gift for holding the attention of restless ten-year-olds. However, they seem to have spent time with one of the rebel bands that were common around here ten years back, and occasionally speak of a coming reign of justice delivered by {GODS}, in a way that does not sound like an ironic joke.
Let the teacher stay. It is good for children to read, and it is not as if they take their elders seriously anyway.
Reading will not help a farmhand plough, but it might goad them into foolish things that get them killed.
Take the teacher aside and say the elder will pay a handsome stipend that will stop abruptly if they breathe a word about politics or worship.
Haunted Dreams

You lie down for a well-deserved nap, but slip into an uneasy dream. You are sailing on a wind-tossed sea. A wave crashes on your bow, sending spray across the decks. You look closely and see that it is not water but blood sloshing around your feet. You stare out over the sea, and the breakers take on the forms of those you have slain in battle.
Have I killed without good reason? I must repent before {GODS}! I shall choose the peaceful path. When there is one, that is...
To where do we sail on this sea of blood? To glory, that is where!
Dreams are but a passing madness. No power speaks to us in this way.
Besiegers' Blues

At first this siege gave your soldiers a welcome respite from the hardships of the march, but now inactivity and boredom have started to take a toll. Even dice and gossip have lost their charms, and you are starting to see quarrels and lapses in discipline.
Drill your soldiers for the coming assault, even though the risk of injury might put several out of action when they are needed most.
March about the camp, searching for specks of rust on blades or sentries who are not fully attentive to their watch. Give any offenders hard, pointless tasks to teach them to keep their standards up.
Let your soldiers enjoy their rest.
Preemptive Work

In your absence, several families in your district have been hard at work draining a marsh and turning it into a field. The survey records in your treasury however show clearly that the marsh is part of your domain. They almost certainly did not know this, but you are entitled to claim the field or charge them for working it.
Transfer ownership to the farmers to encourage such enterprise, even if others may take advantage of you in the future.
Maintain your claim to the land, but allow the farmers to use it for only a token rent.
Demand the land for yourself.
Souvenirs

Some time recently, you are not sure exactly when, your soldiers started a new custom after battle: going about the field collecting grisly trophies from the slain. Now you cannot help noticing these prizes dangling from their belts or from saddle straps.
Tell your soldiers as best you can that, while you respect their spirit, this will frighten local farmers who do not understand warriors' ways.
Take a lively interest in each of these trophies, asking your soldiers at which battle and from which fallen foe they were taken.
Harangue your soldiers for their barbarism, and tell them to honor rather than mock their fallen foes.
Pretend you saw nothing.
Trophies

Some time recently, you are not sure exactly when, your warriors started picking over the field after each battle for grisly trophies from the slain. Now you cannot help noticing the prizes dangling from their belts and from saddle straps.
Tell your warriors as best you can that, while you like their spirit, this will frighten local farmers who do not understand warriors' ways.
Take a lively interest in each of these trophies, asking your warriors at which fight and from which fallen foe they were taken.
Rebuke your warriors for their crude mockery, and tell them a fallen foe has earned respect.
Pretend you saw nothing.
Injury Accident

As you pass through the village streets, a dog dashes out from among some spectators and bites at the heels of one of your {CAVALRYMAN}'s horses, panicking it. The mount rears and gallops down the street, trampling a vegetable vendor who could not get out of its way. The vendor will probably walk with a limp hereafter, and the family demands compensation.
No rider can control a mount that is under attack from a dog. Refuse.
You brought your company into their village, and you must take responsibility.
Tell your {CAVALRYMAN} to sort it out.
Failed Inspection

You take a quick look over your soldiers before you set out, and you are shocked by the state of their gear. In particular, several have frayed straps and shield bindings that look like they might snap in battle. They are supposed to oil and replace their leather at their own expense, and clearly have not been doing so.
Burst into a righteous fury and hand out extra punishments, so that no one will ever again dare neglect their gear.
Sternly lecture them on the risk of a strap snapping in battle. Have them do all their preparations for the march over again, from the beginning.
Buy them the best gear you can find to replace the worn kit.
Pretend you saw nothing.
Hand in the Strongbox

Your clerk at your {WORKSHOP} in {TOWN} has caught one of your overseers skimming from the funds you use to buy raw materials. Luckily, little was taken, and the overseer readily confessed. How do you prevent this from happening in the future?
Make an example of the overseer. Hand them over to the town authorities and urge the full penalty: branding as a thief and exile from the town.
Appeal to your workers' better natures. Plead for leniency for the overseer, and beg the others not to take advantage.
Institute a complex scheme of bookkeeping, even though it will make purchases more onerous and slow down production.
Treat all your workers as potential thieves, and have them searched coming and going from the workshop.
Letter of Reference

As you pass through the market, {NOTABLE.NAME} asks for a minute of your time. A cousin of theirs is planning some business in {TOWN} and would like a letter of reference from you. You know next to nothing about the youth, although {NOTABLE.NAME} swears the cousin is honest and conscientious. You find you are receiving a number of these requests as your fame spreads.
Write truthfully that you do not know much about the bearer of the letter, but they come from a good family.
Write effusively about the bearer's qualities.
Tell {NOTABLE.NAME} that you will write whatever is wanted, for the proper price.
Upbraid {NOTABLE.NAME} in the street for all to hear, for daring to presume you would recommend anyone you do not know.
Nearly a Gift Horse

As you leave {VILLAGE_NAME}, a scraggly youth waves to attract your attention. The youth leads a magnificent {RARE_HORSE} and says it can be yours for a mere 500 in {COIN}. The seller claims to have found it wandering on a heath, almost dead from exhaustion and neglect, and to have nursed it back to health. The seller will not go into town, fearing an unfair accusation of theft.
Plausible enough, and you have no time to check the provenance of every bargain you find. Buy the horse!
A likely story... Place the seller under arrest and send word to the authorities of {TOWN_NAME}, who have the time to sort things out.
You are not sure you trust the seller, but you will not hand them to officials who might just hang them and seize the horse themselves. Go on your way.
Take the horse without paying. Tell the seller that thieves have no right to complain of theft.
A Suitable Match

As you leave the village, a young villager approaches you carrying a months-old baby, surrounded by relatives. They point at one of your soldiers and say that this soldier is the baby's parent, and should stay here and wed. The soldier, strong but not good with words, is too flustered to speak. You can't exactly recall whether you passed through here a year ago or not.
Tell the soldier to search their conscience and do what is right, under the eyes of {GODS}.
Congratulate the soldier on finding a spouse and throw the couple a purse of {COIN} as a wedding gift.
Give your blessing to the marriage and hurl huge handfuls of {COIN} to the villagers, declaring that this will be a day that all shall remember.
Tell the villagers to get themselves a plough horse instead of trying to poach one of your soldiers.
Veterans Demand Privileges

Several of your newer recruits approach you. Your {HIGH_TIER_TROOPS} have been demanding the freshest cuts of meat and the best bread from your stores, leaving the rest to make do with gristle and stale crusts. The veterans say this is the privilege of experience, and that it will push your recruits to improve themselves.
Admonish the {HIGH_TIER_TROOPS} for their indiscipline, even though they will be shamed and may even desert.
Tell your recruits that your veterans have indeed earned the right to the best food.
Tell your soldiers that they have all earned your esteem, and break out an extra ration of {FOOD_OR_DRINK_ITEM} to show your appreciation.
Propose a compromise, a slightly better ration for the veterans, knowing it will avoid a fight but look indecisive.
A Purebred Horse

As you leave the village, one of your riders proudly shows you a new horse bought from a trader. It may not be the fastest beast on four legs, the rider says, but it is strong and spirited; they saw it fighting another of the trader's horses. You look the beast over and see that your rider was sold a mule, its ears cleverly cropped to look like a horse's. The creature is strong enough but far too stubborn to serve as a cavalry mount. Your rider will be the laughingstock of your company for weeks.
Give the rider one of your own horses, add the mule to your pack train, and tell them to come to you before making any more purchases.
Your company could use a laugh. Let the rider show off the prize and take the humiliation, even if it is enough to drive them to desert.
Tell the rider curtly what happened and that they must get the old mount back from the trader, even if it costs them some {COIN}.
Colicky Horses

As you leave town, one of your riders finds their mount lying on the ground, whining in pain and refusing to get up. You are sure the rider was careless and fed the animal too fast after you arrived, eager for a hot meal in town.
Give what care you can, even though it will slow you down and success is far from sure.
Punish the careless rider for their negligence, and let them buy their own remount.
End the animal's misery quickly, and tell the rider you will not trust another poor beast to their care.
The Hermit of the Woods

As you depart the scene of your victory, a figure in plain white robes emerges from a nearby wood. The stranger says you owe your victory to the aid of a healer and wanderer from a century ago, who still helps those who fight in a just cause, and asks that you give half the spoils to {HOLY_PLACE} in gratitude, where it will be used to feed the poor.
Give the spoils of battle as the stranger asks.
Declare that you owe your victory to no wanderer but to your soldiers, and give them the spoils.
Declare that you owe your victory to your own right arm, and keep the spoils.
Fall on your knees in tears, repent of your wrongs, and leave a huge gift.
The Hermit of the Woods

As you depart the scene of your victory, a gaunt figure in black rags creeps out of a nearby wood. The figure says you owe your victory to the hunger of a war-spirit from a century ago, who still favors those who fight for {GODS}, and demands half the plunder for a blood altar in thanks, where it will be used to feed the faithful.
Give the plunder to the blood altar.
Declare that you owe your victory to no spirit but to your warriors, and give them the plunder.
Declare that you owe your victory to your own strong arm, and keep the plunder.
Fall on your knees before the altar, swear fresh oaths, and leave a huge offering.
The Sorcerer's Hoard

As you prepare to leave, one of your soldiers says a villager approached them. There is a particularly ill-tempered sorcerer on the edge of the village who lives not by healing or love-potions but by black magic, and who threatens to curse villagers unless they pay. They asked your soldiers to drive the sorcerer away and burn the hut, and told them they can have the ill-gotten gains.
Convince your soldiers that those who anger sorcerers are likely to see their noses shrivel up or their fingers fall off.
Let them go and demand they split their haul with you.
Tell them that village disputes are a matter for a proper hearing before the elders.
Soldier Wanted for Murder

On your way out of the village, a delegation led by the elder approaches you. They point to a {TROOP_TYPE} in your ranks, a good warrior but none too outgoing. They say the soldier used to farm in this village, but fled after killing a neighbor in a quarrel over boundary stones. The accused snaps back with sudden vehemence: the victim was a cheat, and deserved what came. By law, murder requires the death penalty, though custom allows blood money to be paid instead.
Your {TROOP_TYPE} confessed. There is no option but to let the law take its course.
Tell the villagers that they will have to accept blood money, even though they would prefer vengeance.
Tell the villagers that they will need to wait until the next life for justice, because you need your warrior in this one.
Hunter's Paradise

Your soldiers spot several deer on the outskirts of the village, a rare thing in a land where meat and hides are valuable. The villagers tell you there was an unusual crop of acorns this year, while fear of bandits has kept them from hunting as they normally would. They invite you to shoot a few deer, as there will be plenty to go around anyway and the beasts are trampling the crops.
Free meat, a bit of fun and practice for your soldiers. Sound the hunting horn.
A crowd of loud amateur hunters will scare the game and probably injure themselves. Let your scout bag an animal or two, while the rest of your company marches ahead.
Hunting requires patience. You have real battles to fight.
A Wedding Blessing

As you prepare to leave the village, the elder approaches you. A young relative of the elder is to be married, and it would be a great honor if a warrior of your renown would bless the couple. Your soldiers suppress grins and jostle each other, and you know they are looking forward to the chance to get royally drunk.
Accept the invitation and let your soldiers have their fun.
Accept the invitation, offering a handsome gift to the couple.
Apologize, even though it will disappoint your soldiers.
Sandstorm Warning

As you set out again after the battle, you feel a few scattered drops of rain. Then there is a rush of wind, and a wall of dust engulfs you. The blowing grains sting your face, and you can see but a few arms' lengths ahead. You know how easily soldiers get lost in the notorious sandstorms of the wastes, only to be found later dead of thirst or buried in a dune.
Wait briefly in the lee of a dune until the wind eases up, then press cautiously ahead.
Keep marching, even though there is a good chance some of your soldiers might be separated.
Misplaced Vengeance

Throughout your visit to {VILLAGE}, the villagers were worried that the enemy who sacked {LOOTED_VILLAGE} might be sending patrols their way. As you leave, you find out that their fears were not misplaced. The first thing you see is a flight of ravens in the sky. Your soldiers begin to mutter, but soon they come across a sight that silences them: a pile of burned corpses, stacked by a crossroad, left by the {ENEMY} as their calling card. You press on, but soon notice your soldiers eyeing your prisoners. The prisoners may not have been involved in what happened in {LOOTED_VILLAGE}, but you doubt your soldiers care much.
Take a brief walk to clear your head, and when you come back to find the prisoners gone, do not ask questions.
Tell your soldiers that the prisoners must be kept safe and that you will hold them responsible for anything that happens.
A Love Match

One of your {KNIGHT} asks you for a favor. Their daughter plans to marry someone from the back alleys of this town with a reputation as a no-good layabout. Permission has been refused, but they ask you to do what you can to make sure the two do not elope.
Let them marry. Love must triumph over a parent's pride.
Do your best to explain to the young one that marriages are affairs of the head, not of the heart, and that they had better think of their future and their children's and not elope.
Order your soldiers to give the upstart a sound beating. Who do they think they are, the hero of some foolish romantic song?
Charitable Reputation
As you leave town, you see a much larger number of beggars gathered than you would expect. Some of their limps look unconvincing. Your reputation for compassion and generosity may have gotten around.
If they come to you in need, it is not for you to question them. Have your soldiers hand out alms as usual.

Have some of your soldiers boil up a soup. Keep a watchful eye on all the beggars, especially those who push too eagerly to the front of the line, and serve only those who seem genuinely too frail to work.
Tell them that you are no goose to be plucked. You will reward neither liars nor those who keep company with liars.
A Bandit's Kin

As you leave {VILLAGE_NAME}, a villager steps into your path and grasps your bridle. Among your prisoners is their child, they say. You captured the youth as part of a gang of bandits, but the villager tells you tearfully that the youth is good at heart and fell in with bad company. They swear to make sure the youth never strays from the straight path again.
Release your captive, even if some will mutter that you have a soft heart and a soft head.
Tell the villager that the prisoner shall face the same penalties as any other bandit you caught.
Tell the village that they must pay the ransom, so that all will know there is no profit in banditry.
Nomads Seek a Home

A desperate band of nomads has arrived at your village, seeking a place to settle down. Their herds were ravaged by a sickness, they say, and they are ready to take up farming or work as laborers. Otherwise, they must starve or give themselves to another tribe as servants. The villagers are skeptical. Nomads are too lazy to be farmers, they say, preferring horse theft and feuds.
Welcome them with open arms and a small donation to buy plots of land for their homes.
Sternly instruct them to respect the traditions of settled life, even though the cold welcome might scare some away.
Agree with the villagers that nomads are more trouble than they are worth.
Gold in the Stream

The village is buzzing with a poorly kept secret. After a rare but fierce rainstorm in the dry hills, fishermen have begun to find small flakes of gold in a local stream. If word gets out, there will be a huge influx of fortune-seekers into the area. The gold will last a few months, and it is not clear how much of it will benefit the village or its owner.
This region could use more people. Let word get out.
The village is yours, and so is the gold. Post guards along the river to stop unauthorized prospecting.
Encourage the villagers to mine it quietly, ensuring their cooperation by allowing them to keep it.
Rigging the Market

As you come into town, the merchant {MERCHANT_NAME} makes you an offer. Local merchants are on edge awaiting an incoming caravan from {PLACE}. If you claim that you found its wreckage, looted by bandits, the prices of goods would rise considerably. The merchant offers to pay you 1000 in {COIN}, in addition to whatever extra you can make by selling your own wares once the prices rise.
Accept, but leave enough room for doubt in your account that it won't look too bad if the caravan turns up.
Say you will swear up and down that you saw the wreckage, damaging your reputation, but demand 2000 in {COIN} instead.
Erupt in anger for all to see, and curse {MERCHANT} for taking you for a base liar.
Take a pass on the matter.
Swaggering Sellswords

You are approached by a pair of sellswords. They are anxious to fight for you and ask only that you pay them a token sum. They tell you that a commander like you deserves the services of warriors such as themselves, which is praise to you but a slight to the rest of your company. One of your soldiers tells you these two must have broken their oaths to their old band, or why else would they be so eager to join you?
Take them into your company. Your soldiers will need to bear any insult.
Tell them that you believe them to be oathbreakers, and as such have no place in your ranks.
Tell them they can join you and be as arrogant as they like, so long as they beat one of your soldiers in a duel to first blood.
Through Proper Channels

One of your tenants has a proposal for you. They propose to dig a channel into a hillside, where the water table is high, which will let them flood some low-lying ground and turn it into an oasis garden. The barren hillside is your property, though at present it yields no income of any kind.
Applaud the plan, and tell the tenant that you will charge nothing to sink a channel through your property.
Insist the tenant purchase the hillside from you at market rate.
Wait until the channel is dug and the fields cleared, then charge heavily for the water without which the effort will be for nothing.
Back Taxes

Your reputation as a skilled trader generally does you good, but there is always a downside. When you arrive in {TOWN}, the market inspector comes down from the tower to present you with a list of fees that you supposedly accumulated over the years, based on decrees that go back several centuries. The decrees may be genuine, but in all your talk with merchants, you never heard of anyone ever paying them.
Erupt in fury, telling the inspector that there is no way you will be fleeced in this way, legally or illegally.
Pay, but say for all to hear that selective use of obscure laws is little better than theft.
Reason with the inspector over a splendid dinner and a cask of the finest wine that is of course on you.
Just hand over the {COIN} to make the problem go away.
Water Supplies

In dry country, often the most vulnerable part of a fortress is its water supply. Most depend on wells, but those can run dry. After days spent in front of {FORTRESS_NAME}, you have caught glimpses of the defenders slipping into the hills. You explore where they have gone, and eventually you come across a rough cistern. You suspect that they must be refreshing their water here.
Poison it! Some of the folk of {FORTRESS_NAME} may well perish along with the defenders, but such is war.
The best blows are struck not at the body but at the spirit. Let the defenders know you found it by diverting it to a pool where your soldiers can bathe on the hottest, thirstiest days of the siege.
You respect the defenders' cunning. Simply observe how they slip out of the fortress, by ropes or hidden gates, and learn from it.
The Quiet Life

As you pass through your lands, you see several of your {TROOP_NAME} casting envious eyes over the farmers in the fields. They are tired of wandering from place to place, they say, and hope to put down roots somewhere and start a family. Their term of service is not yet up, but it occurs to you that if they settled in your estates, it would be a boon to your local militia.
Grant their wish, and encourage them to purchase land near {FORTRESS_NAME}.
Give them {COIN} to purchase land near your holding in {VILLAGE_NAME}, so long as they take charge of training the local militia.
Tell them they can go, but only if they forfeit back pay as compensation to you for losing them.
Refuse them permission.
Jobs for the Locals

One prominent resident of {TOWN}, {ARTISAN_NAME}, approaches you. Your {WORKSHOP} has been hiring workers who have recently migrated in from the countryside. The resident asks that you dismiss them and take on some local youths from the back alleys. If you refuse, they will not answer for it when the carts carrying your shipments get snarled in tight gates, slowing down production.
Sadly bid farewell to the migrants and wish them well in future endeavors.
Tell {ARTISAN_NAME} to do their worst; you are not dismissing workers who have served you well.
Ask {ARTISAN_NAME} if you can make a sizeable contribution to the guild's feast and funeral fund.
Tiller and Wanderer

As you are leaving your fief you stumble across an altercation. A group of nomads, who pass by each year on their migration from summer to winter pastures, have let their herds graze in your tenants' crops. Your soldiers far outnumber the nomads and your tenants are urging you to teach them a lesson, but of course their kin might retaliate at a later date.
Seize the nomads' herds to compensate you and your tenants for their crops.
Demand that the nomads pay fair compensation for damaged crops, even though you know this will not settle the problem for long.
Tell the nomads that proud warriors such as themselves need not worry what these dirt-diggers think. Share a meal with them, and see if some will join you.
Hammer of the Sun

As you enter {TOWN_NAME}, one of your {ASERAI_TROOPS} approaches you. Many of their comrades are not used to the heat of the desert, they say. They march after drinking wine through the evening but are not careful to take water through the day, as the sun beats down on them. They have seen soldiers collapse and die from such carelessness and ignorance.
Your soldiers will resent any curbs on their celebrations, even for their own health. Warn them but take no other precautions.
Tell your soldiers that there shall be no wine tonight, and none henceforth until they learn how to handle themselves in the desert.
Let them celebrate, but move slowly in the morning, pausing to make sure that every soldier drinks from their water-skin.
Spoiled Food Supplies

A band of your soldiers comes to you. They show you a heel of bread from your stores, crawling with maggots. A piece of dried meat is streaked with mold. Your quartermaster seems to have packed the goods carelessly, letting damp and vermin get inside.
Money is tight and you have eaten worse in your time. Tell your soldiers to think of it as seasoning.
Order your soldiers to throw away the spoiled food.
Punish the quartermaster for packing it badly, and take the cost of new stores out of the quartermaster's pay. Discipline must prevail.
Wolf down the food yourself and smack your lips, telling your company they are lucky to have such fine rations.
An Affair of Honor

Two of your riders ask leave to fight a duel. Both had been courting the same young merchant in {TOWN}, and one slighted the other in front of the whole street. Some captains encourage duels to feed a fiery pride, but others think such fights erode discipline and, of course, risk injury.
You like that fiery spirit! Let them fight until one falls and cannot rise.
Let them fight until the first blood is drawn.
You will allow no such foolishness. Save their anger for the enemy.
Tell your riders to cast lots and leave the matter to fate.
Veteran Mentor

As you leave the village, a greybeard walks up to you carrying a cudgel. The old warrior is too old to fight now, but still knows a trick: suddenly closing with an opponent and tripping them with a spear. The greybeard offers to teach it to your soldiers for a price, and shows battle-scars that are indeed impressive.
Tell the greybeard that tricks do not win battles, but bravery does.
Accept, even if it costs you time, for a warrior who survived so many battles probably knows a thing or two.
Accept, and have the greybeard demonstrate the technique with a blade on one of your soldiers, so that the lesson sticks.
Camp Fever

As you break camp, you find two of your soldiers bathed in sweat and unable to rouse themselves. They are confused, and one shows pock-marks on the chest. You know the signs of camp fever and fear it will spread fast. Their companions want to tend them, but unless the sick are kept apart, the sickness is likely to spread.
Load the sick onto a cart and give them water, but keep their comrades from them as much as possible.
Send some soldiers to fetch a healer and medicine, accepting that it will delay your march.
Let your soldiers tend the sick as you march.
Servants of Mercy

As the dust of battle settles, you see a band of healers tending the wounded. They say they are the Servants of Hope, wandering folk pledged to help the afflicted in the hope of winning mercy from {GODS}. They offer to travel with your company for a few days and tend your wounded, asking nothing in return.
Tell the healers they will slow you down, and your wounded can mend on their own.
Accept the healers' help.
The Deer Departed

You noticed that the deer around this village are unusually unafraid of people. One of your archers manages to shoot one. The villagers approach afterwards and beg your company not to eat the animal. Their old village seer took the shape of a deer some years ago, they say, and while they cannot tell whether the slain animal is the seer, they want to perform the burial rites properly, just to be sure.
Let the villagers take the deer, even though your soldiers scoff at the superstition.
Let your soldiers enjoy their meal, but commend the villagers for a good attempt at getting hold of a piece of perfectly good meat.
Show genuine remorse and join the burial rites for the deer, just in case, even if your soldiers mutter behind your back.
Soldier in Debt

As you leave town, a merchant approaches you with a document showing that one of your {TROOP_TYPE} took out a loan, to be repaid on departure with a quarter part as interest. The soldier shrugs, calls the merchant a thief for lending at such ruinous rates, and says the money was lost gambling anyway.
Force your soldier to repay the loan with full interest.
Tell the merchant to count themselves lucky not to be chased out of camp for gouging your soldiers.
Pay back the loan from your own purse, even if you earn a name for being easily played.
Boar in a Thicket

As you set out from the village, a local hunter says they can lead you to the nest of a particularly large boar in a nearby thicket. The beast is a threat to the village and too fierce for the hunter, who has already lost two dogs to it. Your soldiers could probably bring it down and claim a meal of fresh pork, though not without risk.
The hunt is on! Ring the thicket with spearmen and drive the boar out.
Leave the beast be.
False Money

As you leave the village, a trader comes to you and says the coins some of your soldiers just paid with are only polished iron. You can indeed see some specks of rust. The trader demands full payment. Your soldiers may well have tried to pass off false coin, but the trader's evidence could as easily have come from the trader's own stock.
Have your soldiers turn out their pockets. If any more false coins turn up, assume they are at fault.
Tell the trader that once a coin is accepted, it is the trader's fault and responsibility.
Vintage of Victory

Among the loot from your last battle you find a vat of fine wine from {WINE_SETTLEMENT_NAME}. You could sell it for a considerable sum, but your soldiers just risked their lives and are not inclined to take {COIN} tomorrow in place of a drink today.
Keep it to sell, telling your company that the money will be spent on keeping them safe.
Break open the wine and let them drink their fill.
Sleeping Sentry

One of your {RECRUIT} fell asleep on guard. The newcomer is not popular, and your soldiers are angry. The sleeper put their lives at risk, and they demand the sentry be handed over to face the old punishment: to run a gauntlet of soldiers with sticks, an ordeal that often ends in death.
Force the recruit to run the gauntlet.
Tell your soldiers to be forgiving, as they were once recruits themselves.
Riddles on the Road

As you leave the village, an old wanderer in rags grabs hold of your sleeve and barks that you must tell what tale the sword tells. Your company gathers in to see whether you will humor this seemingly mad hermit.
That steel is forged from iron, and long hard marches breed tough warriors.
That a sword is all you need, because if you own one, you can take whatever else you need from those without.
That the force of the blade lies only in the hand that wields it.
Laugh madly, tell the wanderer to answer it themselves, and deal a slice that draws blood.
The Pavilion

As you leave town you come across an encampment of traveling entertainers. You see tattered but colorful tents, hear wailing but enticing music, and smell cheap incense and meat that is probably slightly spoiled but spiced so you would never notice. A troupe in some noble's thrown-away silks, their faces skillfully made up with charcoal and sheep's blood, beckons to your soldiers. What do you do?
Tell your soldiers to steer clear of such dubious enticements.
Let your soldiers have some fun, but tell them to watch their purses and stay out of fights.
The fun is on you! Hurl a fistful of {COIN} at the entertainers and tell them your soldiers deserve nothing but the best.
Rob the entertainers. Their wealth is surely ill-gotten, and to whom will they complain?
Turnpike

You notice a footpath leading through your holding that could quickly be improved for wagons and made a shortcut between the main trade roads. You could charge tolls and turn it into a turnpike, though the locals would resent the added traffic and fees on their customary route.
Widen the road for wagons but charge tolls to use it.
Improve the road, but charge no tolls.
Let it be.
Conflict Over Commons

Grazing land has grown scarce near {TOWN_OR_CASTLE_NAME}, and a heath between {POORER_VILLAGE} and {RICHER_VILLAGE}, covered with thistle and once of little value, has become a point of contention. {POORER_VILLAGE} claims that they have grazed goats there for generations, but {RICHER_VILLAGE} has produced a document showing rightful title.
The laws of the realm are clear: however many years go by, the first owner keeps the land unless it is lawfully sold or given away.
You hold to the old principle: the land belongs to the earth, not to any people, and goes to those who make the best use of it.
Have them split it.
Let them know that your decision is for sale at a price.
Wages of War and Diseases

Between the wars and an epidemic, the villages near {FIEF_NAME} are short of people, especially the young. Fields are going fallow for lack of hands to plough them, especially those cleared only in recent generations where title is in dispute. As holder of this land, you can redistribute it, but you will need to find labor.
Seize the land as your own, drawing desperate peasants from the surrounding districts with exploitative sharecropping terms.
Give the land to some of your veterans as a reward for their service.
Hand out money to the region's farmers so they can hire laborers or give their children generous marriage gifts.
Speculative Investment

You strike up a conversation with a trader in town who is desperate for news of the wars. When you mention the looting of {VILLAGE_NAME}, the trader makes a proposition. The price of grain will almost certainly rise, and the trader means to buy up food now and sell it when hunger hits. Money is needed, so you are offered {OTHER_GOOD} at far below their market value of 1000 in {COIN}, if you keep this to yourself.
All is fair in trade and war. You accept the deal.
Tell the trader quietly that you will not profit from the misery of others.
Denounce the trader angrily in public as a food hoarder, so that word of your compassion and mercy gets around.
Ill-Conceived Plans

Several of your {TROOP_TYPE} have an idea for the next battle. They suggest hiding in a supply wagon and being left for the enemy to find and drag into camp, whereupon they will leap out and wreak havoc. They are very proud of their scheme, even though you can think of half a dozen reasons it will not work.
Tell them that every people has its own legend about warriors hidden in unlikely places, and you cannot imagine them getting away with it.
Let them test the plan. Buy a hide, sew them into it with their weapons, and gather the company to watch in amusement as they struggle free.
Nod quickly as though you were not listening and move on to some other task.
Dodgy Spice

Merchants are savvy to most attempts to pass off shoddy goods as top quality, but one of your {TROOP.NAME} knows a few tricks that are not in the usual rogue's repertoire. The plan: buy a selection of spices from the market, then sprinkle a bit of pomegranate rind in with the saffron, some cassia bark with the cinnamon, and a lead compound called litharge with the pepper.
A bit of lead never hurt anyone! Try them all, and split the profits with your {TROOP.NAME}.
You vaguely recall hearing that lead might be poisonous, but you will try the others.
Tell your soldier to save that ingenuity for battle, not trade.
Thank your soldier curtly and try the trick, but pay nothing.
Third-Party Arbitration

Knowing your reputation as a trader, two merchants in {TOWN_NAME} ask you to arbitrate a dispute. They drew up a contract giving each a half-share in an incoming shipment of wine. When it arrived, the ship's captain demanded twice the price. The wealthier partner was at the docks, took the initiative and bought the goods, accepting a loss to protect a name as a reliable supplier to the local taverns, but the other partner is poorer and wants out of the deal.
The letter of the contract favors the wealthier partner. Merchants should be careful what they sign.
Never mind the letter of the contract: the reasonable, decent course for the richer merchant would have been to consult the partner.
Tell them that the whole thing gives you a headache.
Let the wealthier merchant know that your decision is for sale.
Mining

After studying the ground around {FORTRESS_NAME}, you think conditions might suit mining: digging a tunnel under a wall, then collapsing it. This can open a breach but is slow and risky. If you hit rock underground, your efforts go to waste. If the ground is too soft, the tunnel may collapse and bury your soldiers. Most troops are reluctant to spend time in dark, cramped tunnels unless they are paid extra, or forced.
Double the pay of any soldiers willing to dig the mine, and tunnel carefully.
Tunnel quickly, threatening to execute anyone who refuses for insubordination.
Rely on the usual methods.
The Workers Walk Out

Trade in {TOWN_NAME} has been booming, and prices and wages are rising. The workers at your {WORKSHOP} have taken notice. Your overseer reports that they have all refused to come in until they get a raise. Plenty of hungry mouths and willing hands remain in town, but the current workers might cause trouble if they are replaced.
Chide them gently for walking off the job before coming to you first, because of course you will raise their wages.
Sit down with them and negotiate a mutual understanding.
Dismiss the lot of them, hire new workers, and post some soldiers outside to protect your shop.
Respect for the Slain

Throughout your visit to {VILLAGE}, one of your older {TROOP_TYPE} seems moody and downcast. As you march out, the old soldier suddenly stops, stares at a roadside stall, then breaks from your column and starts shouting at the vendor. The story tumbles out. They fought in a battle here against {NEAREST_OTHER_CULTURE}, and the vendor is selling scraps of metal clearly looted from the graves of the dead.
Buy what old helmets and shield bosses you can and let your soldier build a small memorial on the battlefield, even though you know it will soon be looted afresh.
Do you not loot whatever you can from the dead after your victories? Tell your soldier to save that anger for wrongs done to the living.
Erupt in fury at the vendor and accuse them of grave robbing. The thefts will probably not stop, but your soldiers will be pleased.
Cries in the Mist

The people of {VILLAGE_NAME} warned you to take care outside their village. When the mist gathers, the woods are haunted by spirits whose shrieks foretell death. Now the gloom is gathering, and you hear mutterings from your soldiers. You are certain they will soon hear wailing and see apparitions, real or imagined. The mounts are growing twitchy too, picking up the mood, and accidents are likely.
Tell your soldiers to ignore the superstitions of villagers, and press on.
Drive off the spirits in the proper way, by loudly calling on {GODS} to ward off the ghosts of the dark.
Appease the spirits as the villagers advised, by slaughtering a black cockerel they sold to one of your soldiers.
Desperate Times

As you pass through the town gates, a crowd of refugees from the countryside throngs around you. They are gaunt, with sunken eyes. They say they could not sow their fields this year for fear of raiders, and were forced to eat their seed grain. They beg for any scraps you can spare.
Break out your food and let them fill their bellies before you depart
Give them enough money to replace their seed grain, even though the townsfolk may complain that it raises prices
Tell them that you cannot help
Desperate Times

As you pass through the town gates, a crowd of starving wretches from the countryside throngs around you. They are gaunt, with sunken eyes. They say raiders kept them from sowing this year, and they ate their seed grain. They beg for any scraps you can spare.
Break out your food and let them eat before you move on
Throw them enough {COIN} to buy seed grain, though the townsfolk will grumble that prices rise
Tell them you have nothing to spare
Fight over an Insult

A fight breaks out in your camp. A proud {CAVALRYMAN} ordered a {FOOTMAN} to water the horses, even though the {FOOTMAN} is a veteran nearly twice the {CAVALRYMAN}'s age. The two traded insults, and now the {FOOTMAN} demands a duel while the {CAVALRYMAN}, who will duel only an equal, demands that the {FOOTMAN} be told to keep to their place.
Only blood can wipe out an insult! Let the two have it out, until one falls and cannot rise
Reprimand the rider, even though they are fiery and might desert
Reprimand the veteran, who will grumble but has the sense to swallow their pride
Tell them both to stop behaving like fools
Horsefly Plague

One of your riders reports that some horses seem strangely weak. You see their listless eyes and swollen bellies and recognize it: swamp fever. Horseflies spread this plague, and it will infect other animals unless the sick horse is killed.
Isolate the infected horses at once to stop the spread
Order the infected horses put down to avoid further contamination
Ignore the outbreak and keep marching
Bloody Flux

As you inspect your siege camp, you find disgusting proof that one or more of your soldiers has the bloody flux. It will pass between soldiers who share food and water, and you know what it can do to a besieging army if left unchecked.
Identify the sick and make them camp outside your palisades, tending to themselves.
Treat your soldiers but trust in strict measures, like digging latrines outside camp and sending them far afield for water, which they are likely to resent.
Treat the sick and make no further demands on your soldiers, trusting in luck to see you through.
Right of Plunder

As you prepare to march from newly captured {TOWN_NAME}, your soldiers stop you. They shed their blood in your war, and you denied them the customary right to sack the town. They say that if you will not let them take their reward from the enemy, you should reward them from your own purse.
Let your soldiers go back and sack the town while it is still defenseless
Pay them yourself
Punish the troublemakers for stirring up mutiny
Remind your soldiers that mercy to the innocent is a duty owed to {GODS}
Right of Plunder

As you prepare to march from newly taken {TOWN_NAME}, your soldiers block the road. They bled for your war, and you denied them their plunder. They say that if you will not let them loot the enemy, you can pay them from your own purse.
Let your soldiers go back and sack the town while it is still defenseless
Pay them yourself
Punish the troublemakers for stirring up mutiny
Order your soldiers to spare the townsfolk: the living pay tribute, the dead pay nothing
Wedding Celebration

As you break camp, several of your veterans come forward, looking sheepish. They push one of their number forward and say that this one married a young lass in the last village you visited. They ask if they may share one of the casks of wine they have noticed you carrying, in celebration.
Indulge your soldiers, even though you have little doubt that the wedding is an invention
Tell them that you will not reward deceit
Pour all your wine onto the ground, telling them that you will not tolerate anything that erodes their morals and discipline
Wild Apples

As you enter the village, some of your soldiers tell you they have found a stand of wild apple trees in full bloom by a stream. The fruit would fetch a fine price in the village market. The land seems to belong to no one, but you know that once the trees are discovered, a half-dozen claimants will press their title.
Tell your soldiers to help themselves.
Tell the villagers of your discovery
Broken-down Wagon
You come across a trader whose wagon is stuck in the road after the draught horse went lame. The trader is desperate to sell the wares before they spoil, and offers them at a bargain price.
Give the trader a draught animal so they can continue on their way.
Sell the trader your cheapest horse so they can continue.
Buy the wares at the bargain price.
Explain that you cannot help.
Coin Clipping

Shortly after the loot is shared out, you find several of your soldiers rubbing the edges of the coins you paid them against a rock. You know what they are doing: clipping, shaving off a bit of the silver to melt down in the hope that no one notices.
Turn a blind eye, even though the practice is little better than counterfeiting
Order your soldiers to stop, and warn the merchants in the next town to look very carefully at any coins your soldiers give them.
Show them a few tricks from your own bag of dirty tricks
No Time to Mourn

It is time to bury your dead, but the ground is frozen solid and the wood from nearby trees is too wet to make a proper pyre. You can give the bodies a hasty burial in a gully, even though wolves or other beasts may find them, or carry the bodies with you and bury them as soon as you can.
Carry the bodies with you until you find dry wood or softer ground
Cover the bodies as best you can and hope for the best
Trade Proposal

A passing trader offers to buy {GOOD} from your company at well over the price it would fetch in the nearest town. No doubt some other merchant has fed the trader bad information on prices, either to ruin a rival or as a joke.
Traders should know their trade. Keep silent and take the offer
Tell the trader that you have no wish to profit from their ignorance
A fool and their money are soon parted: save the trader some time. Haggle for more
A Deadly Reputation
As you leave the village, a merchant who clearly wants your approval shouts out, "{LOCAL_KING} has slain thousands, but {PLAYER} tens of thousands!"
I have, and it is but a taste before the main feast.
All I have done has been in the service of {KING}. I am but their will made flesh.
Any blood I have shed may have been necessary, but I pray to {GODS} for forgiveness.
Acknowledge the merchant by howling like a beast and swirling your weapon about, as mad behavior makes for good stories.
Abundance of Troublemakers

As you prepare to leave, the village elder approaches you. A gang of four youths keeps picking fights with the other villagers, the elder says. Even their own families do not want them around, for fear they will kill someone and start a blood feud. The elder begs you to take them into your ranks, where they can learn a bit of discipline.
Accept the recruits. At the first chance, find fault with their gear and give them a sound thrashing, so they learn to mend their ways.
Take the recruits. Try not to be too hard on them at first, even though they will probably wear down your company's discipline.
Tell the elder to find some other way to handle the troublemakers.
Indebted Farmers

Several freeholding farmers on your lands have fallen into debt through a mix of bad luck and risky ventures: a plough horse that died, a crop ruined by frost. They cannot pay their dues, and ask for a reprieve of several years.
You know an opportunity when you see one. Seize their lands. They can farm as your tenants
Grant a reprieve, but tack on a bit of interest so that you are not swamped with hard luck stories
Call in a favor with a moneylender in town to reduce their debts so they can pay their dues
Help them get back on their feet, even if some say that you are too trusting
Conflict over Commons

Villagers from your fief of {VILLAGE} have started going to a marsh on the road to {VILLAGE2} to gather reeds for baskets, adding to their earnings. Hunters from {VILLAGE2}, held by {LORD.NAME}, say the villagers have been disturbing the local waterfowl. Neither of you holds title to the marsh, but {VILLAGE2} says its people went there first. Your tenants say it is not their problem if they have found a better use for the land.
Keep sending your reed gatherers there, and have them bring staves and slings to defend their rights
Tell {NOBLE.NAME} that your people will get their reeds elsewhere and stop frightening off the game.
Successful Harvest

An early thaw and a warm spring have brought a bumper crop, which the prayers of the villagers and the efforts of the local cats have kept safe from rats and birds. Such bounty is rare. What will you do?
Feast! Give thanks to {GODS} and the spirits of the land, and make merry
Encourage the farmers to sell the crops and make much-needed improvements to irrigation and roads
Go through your accounts to see who might owe you back dues
Mad Dog

Your soldiers are very proud of you, perhaps too proud. Every time they go into town, they spread exaggerated tales of your recklessness in battle. You imagine this could win you a few admiring recruits, but more and more you catch a look of fear or distrust, as though you were a wild beast or a monster.
Let the tales spread! Sanity and caution do not inspire legend
In a towering rage, tell your soldiers that you will not tolerate lies of any sort.
Try to play down the image of a raving lunatic by being as friendly as possible on your next visit to town.
Heat and Dust

Your soldiers did not expect to spend so long in the desert. They complain that baggage they would gladly carry in normal times becomes a crushing burden when the blazing sun is high in the sky. They have found camels for sale in the markets and ask you to buy them to lighten their loads.
Agree to buy the camels.
Tell them that you need the money for other purposes.
Sorrows of War

As you leave {TOWN_NAME}, a young woman throws herself in front of you. She raises her face to the sky, tears at her hair, and wails that her young husband took up arms for you and was slain in battle. "You took him from me!" she screams. It is not clear what she wants.

Tell her, as soberly as you can, that her husband gave his life for a worthy cause. Hand her a purse of 100 {COIN}, and say you are sure he would be glad if she wed again, as long as he remains in her memory.
Dismount, burst into tears, take her hands in yours and say that every life lost in your service tears at your heart, and that you want nothing more than for these wars to end.
Tell her that all must bear their fate with dignity, for such is the will of {GODS}.
Have your purser speak to her at length about what she might need, as you keep your distance.
Sorrows of War

As you leave {TOWN_NAME}, a young woman blocks your path. She raises her face to the sky, tears at her hair, and wails that her young husband marched with you and was slain in battle. "You took him from me!" she screams. It is not clear what she wants.
Tell her gruffly that her husband fell in service to {GODS}. Toss her a purse of 100 {COIN}, and say that he would want her to wed again, as long as she remembers him.
Dismount, take her hands in yours and say that every life lost in your service weighs on you, and that you want nothing more than for these wars to end.
Tell her to bear her loss in silence; such is the will of {GODS}.
Have your purser speak to her at length about what she might need, as you keep your distance.
Tipping the Scales

Your company is taking longer than usual to get ready, and you have time to relax and watch the goings-on at the market. One vendor in particular catches your eye. The vendor always uses one set of weights for the sacks bought from local farmers, and another for the goods sold. You have little doubt that one or both of these sets is a false measure, used to cheat customers.
This is not your affair, and other merchants or corrupt officials may be in on it. Walk away.
Denounce the merchant loudly, even at the risk of making enemies among the town's leading folk.
Walk up to the merchant and insist on the lighter weights to buy one measure of goods. Then come back later and return it, insisting on the heavier weights.
At the Breach

You have studied the walls of {FORTRESS_NAME} for days, and in one place you see what looks like a crack, perhaps from an old earthquake, or just neglect. It is hard to hit with your siege engines and the ground is too rocky to mine, but you reckon soldiers with pickaxes alone could bring it down, if they would brave the storm of arrows and stones that would pour from the battlements above.
A purse of {COIN} for every stone brought to me from that wall!
Order your recruits to swarm the base of the wall and bring it down. They can be replaced.
A breach is not worth the losses.
Occupational Safety

Business is good at your {WORKSHOP} in {TOWN}, but in the rush to keep up with demand the usual precautions are being skipped. {INJURY_TEXT} The worker will live, but is unlikely to do skilled work again, and the rest of the workers fear future accidents.
Pay the injured worker a pension and order your supervisors to take more care, even if it slows down production.
You will not pay for another's clumsiness. Let work go on at the same pace.
As on the battlefield, so on the workshop floor. Let each team work at its own pace, earning bonuses for output but taking responsibility for injuries.
Just Rewards

Your soldiers fought heroically in the last battle. As they help their wounded comrades back to camp and gather the slain, their weary faces sometimes turn to you with expectation. If ever there was a time to give them some extra recognition of their valor and sacrifice, this would be it.
Reach into your treasury and grab great fistfuls of {COIN}, hurling it to your soldiers and praising them by name for their deeds.
Give them an extra week's pay as a bonus, telling them they deserve far more but it is all you can afford.
Gruffly tell them that you were pleased they did their duty.
Feeling the Bite

As you leave {VILLAGE_NAME}, several villagers approach you. They warn that stagnant ponds left by the last rain have yet to dry and have bred mosquitos. They offer to sell you a concoction of oils including rosemary, catmint and other herbs that they say will ward off all flying vermin.
Buy vials of ointment for everyone in your company, at the risk of looking gullible.
Have your soldiers wrap themselves up as best they can and press on.
Take roundabout routes to avoid the ponds.
